facts.raw_span: A 73-year-old man
no compressive symptoms or systemic complaints
Physical examination was unremarkable
hematocrit 25.7% (normal 38–52%)
hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL (normal 13–18 g/dL)
red-cell count 3.84 × 10^6/mm^3 (normal 4.0–5.5 × 10^6/mm^3)
platelet count 88,000/mm^3 (normal 160,000–410,000/mm^3)
white-cell count 7000/mm^3 (normal 3800–8500/mm^3) with 58.3% neutrophils, 9.0% lymphocytes, and 25% eosinophils (normal 0–7%)
dysplastic megakaryocytes and erythrocytes without an increased number of blast cells
a 38-mm oval, well-encapsulated mass in the posterior mediastinum
the lesion had moderate signal intensity on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted images
the radiographic findings were not typical for neurogenic tumors

concepts.why: The patient's laboratory studies show cytopenias, including anemia, thrombocytopenia, and a low red-cell count, and the bone marrow smear reveals dysplastic megakaryocytes and erythrocytes, consistent with myelodysplastic syndrome.

The patient's bone marrow smear shows dysplastic megakaryocytes and erythrocytes without an increased number of blast cells, consistent with refractory cytopenia with multilineage dysplasia, a subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome.

The patient has a well-encapsulated mass in the posterior mediastinum, which is not typical for neurogenic tumors, suggesting a possible diagnosis of a posterior mediastinal mass or mediastinal tumor.
The patient's mass in the posterior mediastinum could be a germ cell tumor, which can present as a well-encapsulated mass in the mediastinum.
The patient's mass in the posterior mediastinum could be a thymoma, which can present as a well-encapsulated mass in the mediastinum.
